Random Variables, Expectation/Variance and MGF
Random Variable
Let (Ω, S) be a sample space. A finite single-valued function that
maps Ω into < is called a random variable (RV) if the inverse
images under X of all Borel sets in < are events, that is, if
X−1
(B) = {ω : X(ω) ∈ B} ∈ S, for all B ∈ B.
A RV is a numerical description of the outcome of an
experiment.
A variable that takes on different values as a result of the
outcomes of a random experiment.
The set of all values which X takes up may be discrete or
continuous, and accordingly the RV is said to be
discrete/continuous.
There do exist subsets of < that do not belong to B, and hence
there exist real-valued functions defined on Ω that are not RVs.
Dr. Chanchal Kundu RGIPT, Jais Campus

Example 
The Statistical Abstract of the United States is published 
annually. It contains a wide variety of information based on 
the census as well as other sources. The objective is to 
provide information about a variety of different aspects of 
the lives of the country’s residents. One of the questions 
asked households to report the number of color televisions in 
the household. The following table summarizes the data. 
Develop the probability distribution of the random variable 
defined as the number of color televisions per household.

Dr. Chanchal Kundu RGIPT, Rae Bareli
Example 
.
Number of Color Televisions Number of Households (1,000s)
0 1,218
1 32,379
2 37,961
3 19,387
4 7,714
5 2,842
Total 101,501

Dr. Chanchal Kundu RGIPT, Rae Bareli
Example 
Probability distributions can be estimated from relative 
frequencies. 
1,218 ÷ 101,501 = 0.012
e.g. P(X=4) = P(4) = 0.076 = 7.6%

Random Variables, Expectation/Variance and MGF
Variance of a Random Variable X:
The second central moment µ2 is of great importance and is called the
variance of X written as V ar(X), i.e.,
V ar(X) = µ2 = E{(X − µ)
2} = σ
2
, say.
• A measure of the dispersion or variability in the random variable.
• A weighted average of the squared deviations from the mean µ.
Variance is a characteristic which describes how widely the probability
masses are spread about the mean or, in otherwords, an inverse
measure of concentration of the probability masses about the mean. It
is called a measure of dispersion. It represents the moment of inertia
of the probability mass distribution about a line through the mean
perpendicular to the line of the distribution.

2 = α2 − µ

2 = E{X(X − 1)} − µ(µ − 1)
